n: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian, naming the rulers of the time. The fifteenth year of Emperor Tiberius was about AD 28-29. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee, and his brother Philip ruled lands to the northeast.

f.g: Roman emperor AD 14-37, successor of Augustus.
A ruler of part of a kingdom, below the rank of king.

n: Annas, the former high priest, still held great influence while his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office. Then God’s word came to John in the wilderness — not to the powerful names just listed.

f.g: Annas was deposed by Rome in AD 15 but remained powerful; Caiaphas served about AD 18-36.

f.w: the word of God came unto John

n: John traveled throughout the Jordan valley, preaching a baptism that showed repentance, for the forgiveness of sins.

This fulfilled Isaiah’s words about a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the Lord’s way. The JST adds a passage here about Christ coming to take away the sins of the world and bring salvation to the Gentiles.

f.w: The voice of one crying in the wilderness

n: Isaiah pictured road builders preparing a highway for a king: filling valleys, leveling hills, straightening curves. Spiritually, hearts must be made ready for Christ.
Then all humanity will see God’s salvation. Luke, writing for Gentiles, extends the quotation to include this universal promise.
John spoke bluntly to the crowds: you brood of snakes! Who warned you to run from the coming judgment? He wanted real change, not just a ritual.

f.g: Offspring of poisonous snakes — fleeing a fire, as snakes do from a burning field.

n: Show by your actions that you’ve truly repented. Don’t rely on being Abraham’s descendants — God could make children of Abraham out of these stones. Lineage alone saves no one.

f.w: We have Abraham to our father

n: The axe is already at the root. Every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit will be cut down and burned. Judgment is near.

f.w: the axe is laid unto the root

n: The crowds asked: then what should we do? John’s answers, found only in Luke, are practical.
Share what you have. If you have two shirts, give one to someone who has none; do the same with food. Repentance shows up in generosity.
Tax collectors also came to be baptized and asked what they should do.

f.g: Tax collectors, often notorious for overcharging.

n: Collect no more than you’re required to. Be honest in your work.
Soldiers asked too. John said: don’t extort money by threats or false accusations, and be content with your pay.

f.g: Don’t shake people down for money.

n: People were filled with expectation, and everyone wondered whether John might be the Messiah.
John answered: I baptize with water, but someone far greater is coming — I’m not worthy to untie his sandals. He will baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire.

f.w: with the Holy Ghost and with fire

n: His winnowing fork is in his hand to clear his threshing floor. He’ll gather the wheat into his barn and burn the chaff — a picture of separating the righteous from the wicked.

f.g: A winnowing fork, used to toss grain so the wind blows away the husks.

n: With many other appeals, John preached the good news to the people.
But Herod Antipas, rebuked by John for marrying his brother’s wife Herodias and for his other evil deeds…
…added this to all his wrongs: he locked John up in prison. Luke tells this before the baptism of Jesus to finish John’s story.
When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was also baptized. While he was praying, heaven opened. Luke often highlights Jesus at prayer.
The Holy Ghost came down on him in bodily form like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, “You are my beloved Son; I am well pleased with you.” Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are all present.

Jesus was about thirty when he began his ministry — the age priests began full service. People assumed he was Joseph’s son; Luke traces the line back through Heli. Many scholars think this genealogy follows Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

f.g: Luke signals that Joseph was not Jesus’ biological father.

n: Luke’s genealogy runs backward, from Jesus to Adam — unlike Matthew’s, which runs forward from Abraham. These first names are otherwise unknown ancestors from the centuries after the exile.

f.g: One of many little-known names preserved only here.

n: More unknown ancestors. Their obscurity is part of the message: Jesus came through ordinary families.

f.g: A common Jewish name meaning “gift of the Lord.”

n: The line continues through ordinary Jews whose names appear nowhere else in scripture.
Zerubbabel and Shealtiel appear — leaders of the Jews who returned from Babylon and rebuilt the temple. They are also in Matthew’s list.

f.g: Zerubbabel, governor who led the rebuilding of the temple after the exile.

n: These names reach back into the period of the kings of Judah and the exile, though not through the royal line.

f.g: Not the same as Judah’s son Er in Genesis.

n: Another run of names, including Joshua (Jose) and another Levi, otherwise unrecorded.
Names here echo the tribal patriarchs — Simeon, Judah, Joseph — common names among faithful Israelite families.
Luke traces Jesus through Nathan, a son of David, rather than through Solomon and the kings as Matthew does. Either way, Jesus is a true son of David.

f.g: A son of David and Bathsheba, brother of Solomon.

n: From David back through Jesse, Obed, and Boaz (husband of Ruth), to Salmon and Nahshon, a leader of Judah in Moses’ day.

f.g: Boaz, who married Ruth the Moabite.
Nahshon, chief of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness.

n: Back through the tribe of Judah: Amminadab, Ram, Hezron, Perez, and Judah himself, son of Jacob.

f.g: Perez, son of Judah and Tamar.

n: The covenant patriarchs: Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, then Terah and Nahor. Jesus is the promised seed of Abraham.
Before Abraham, the line runs through the descendants of Shem listed in Genesis: Serug, Reu, Peleg, Eber (ancestor of the Hebrews), and Shelah.

f.g: Eber, possibly the source of the name “Hebrew.”

n: Here Luke includes a second Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah, following the Greek Old Testament. Then Shem, Noah, and Lamech.

f.g: This Cainan appears in the Greek Septuagint version of Genesis 11 but not the Hebrew text.

n: The antediluvian (pre-flood) patriarchs: Methuselah, Enoch, Jared, Mahalaleel, and Cainan (Kenan). Latter-day Saint scripture tells much more about Enoch and his city of Zion.
Finally Enos, Seth, Adam — and God. By tracing Jesus to Adam, “the son of God,” Luke shows that Jesus came for all of humanity, not just Israel.

f.w: Adam, which was the son of God
